Cell Energy 3D Lab

Photosynthesis and cellular respiration happen inside cells too small to see, so they are hard to picture. These four labs let you run a real experiment on a 3D lab bench, then shrink down inside a leaf, a chloroplast and a mitochondrion to see where the energy goes. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

🌿 Photosynthesis (chloroplasts)

6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂

Light energy is stored as chemical energy in the bonds of glucose. Plants, algae and some bacteria do this.

🔥 Cellular respiration (mitochondria)

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ATP)

Cells break glucose apart and capture the energy as ATP. Plants and animals do this, all day and all night.

3D lab furniture and equipment (cabinets, lamp, lab bottles, vials, clock, stools, safety glasses, sink, first-aid cabinet, extinguisher, SDS binder, steel table): NVIDIA SimReady assets, licensed under CC BY 4.0; converted from OpenUSD and simplified for offline use. Teacher notes

Four self-contained labs in one offline HTML file. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks included). Nothing is uploaded; results tables are saved in the browser on that device only. Students can download their data as a CSV.

Suggested sequence (3–4 class periods)

  • Lab 1 (1 period): controlled experiment — independent variable lamp distance, dependent variable bubbles per minute, three trials and a mean, graph against light intensity. Extensions: NaHCO₃ (CO₂) level, filter color, water temperature.
  • Lab 2 (½–1 period): limiting factors and stomata; the six grower challenges check reasoning.
  • Lab 3 (½ period): chloroplast structure; light-dependent reactions → ATP/NADPH → Calvin cycle. Light-off and CO₂-off predictions.
  • Lab 4 (½–1 period): glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain, ATP yield; oxygen-off and sprint scenarios for fermentation.

What the models assume

  • Lab 1: light intensity follows the inverse-square law (relative units: 100 at 15 cm). Bubble rate rises with light and levels off when CO₂ (NaHCO₃) becomes limiting; it rises with temperature to about 30 °C, falls above that and stops when enzymes denature (sprig is damaged above about 44 °C). The plant also respires, so very dim light gives no bubbles. Bubble counts vary from trial to trial, like a real plant.
  • Lab 4 counts about 32 ATP per glucose with oxygen (2 glycolysis + 2 Krebs + about 28 from the electron transport chain) and 2 ATP per glucose without it. Textbooks quote 30–38; modern estimates are about 30–32.
  • All numbers are simplified for teaching. They show the right patterns, not real measurements.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-LS1-5 (photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy), HS-LS1-7 (cellular respiration and net energy transfer), HS-LS2-5 (carbon cycling). Middle school: MS-LS1-6, MS-LS1-7. Practices: planning and carrying out investigations; analyzing and interpreting data; developing and using models.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42): B.11A (matter conserved and energy transferred in photosynthesis and cellular respiration, using models and chemical equations); B.11B (role of enzymes in cellular processes).
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.3 (follow a multistep experimental procedure, taking measurements); RST.9-10.7 (translate between words, tables and graphs).
  • AP Biology: Unit 3 Cellular Energetics — 3.5 Photosynthesis, 3.6 Cellular Respiration (use the “Deeper” views in Labs 3 and 4).

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan. Gray buttons explain why they cannot be used yet when you tap them.
